title: Double-tap Withdraw: 'you can't go negative'
topic: A wallet check that only works one click at a time
blurb: The user has $100 and mashes Withdraw $80 twice. The AI says the balance check makes that impossible.
prompt: An AI wrote this Node.js withdrawal handler for a wallet app. A user with $100 double-taps 'Withdraw $80'. Find the bug before it ships.

segments.label: L6
segments.text: return { ok: true, balance: balance - amount };

conclusion: AI summary: We check `balance < amount` before writing, so the balance can never go negative. Ship it.

flaws.original: const updated = await db.atomicDebitIfEnough(userId, amount); // atomic conditional update / transaction

diagnosis_choices.label: Race condition: two taps both read $100, pass L4, and overwrite with $20 — withdrawing $160.
JavaScript is single-threaded, so `await` blocks every other request until `withdraw` resolves.
Without a `try/catch` around `setBalance`, a network blip doubles the deduction on retry.
`balance - amount` concatenates strings when `db.getBalance` returns a numeric string from SQL.

fix_choices.label: Use an atomic DB update: `UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?`.
Drop `await` on L5 so `setBalance` runs synchronously before the next tap enters the event loop.
Re-read `db.getBalance(userId)` a second time right before `setBalance` to confirm the $100.
Wrap `setBalance` in `try/catch` and change L4 from `balance < amount` to `balance <= amount`.

flaws.explanation: Each `await` yields back to the event loop. Two simultaneous $80 withdrawals both read `balance = 100`, both pass the check, and both write `20` — letting the user spend $160 from a $100 wallet.
flaws.why_tempting: Developers assume 'Node.js is single-threaded' means no race conditions, forgetting that async I/O interleaves between `await` points.
flaws.catch_rule: Whenever you see `read -> await -> check -> await -> write` on shared money or quota, demand an atomic conditional update or DB transaction.
flaws.hint: Imagine both taps pausing after they read the balance, before either one writes.

practice.problem: A drop has `left = 1`. Two fans hit Buy at the same instant using `get` then `set(left - 1)`. What happens?
practice.answer: Both read `1`, both succeed, and two people just bought the last item.

clean_conclusion: The database checks and deducts in one step, so two taps can't both sneak through.

diagnosis: Declaring `withdraw` as `async` lets callers ignore the returned Promise and skip `await`.
Passing `db` as the third argument reopens a new database connection on every withdrawal.
In Node.js, `async` functions spawn a new OS thread per call, which causes `amount` to race.
Missing default `amount = 0` throws ReferenceError when a user taps too fast.
fix: Remove `async` from the signature so withdrawals execute synchronously.
Create a single global `db` inside `withdraw` instead of passing it in.
Set `amount = 0` as a default parameter on line 1.
Return a boolean instead of a Promise from `withdraw`.

diagnosis: Checking `amount <= 0` lets `NaN` slip through because `NaN <= 0` evaluates to `false`.
Throwing an Error inside an `async` function crashes the Node process instead of rejecting.
Using `<=` rejects valid zero-fee test withdrawals that check wallet connectivity.
`amount <= 0` compares against `0` instead of checking `amount > 100`.
fix: Change to `if (!(amount > 0))` so `NaN` is caught too.
Return `{ ok: false }` instead of throwing an Error inside an `async` function.
Change `<=` to `<` so zero-dollar checks pass.
Validate `amount <= 100` right on line 2.

diagnosis: Using `const balance` freezes the value so line 5 can't subtract `amount` from it.
`await db.getBalance(userId)` blocks the whole Node event loop until SQL replies.
Reading `balance` without `Number(...)` treats `$100` as a string on line 4.
Missing `await` on `userId` lets two users read each other's balance.
fix: Change `const balance` to `let balance` so line 5 can decrement it.
Cast `const balance = Number(await db.getBalance(userId));`.
Cache `balance` in a module-level variable to skip the `await`.
Drop `await` on line 3 so `getBalance` doesn't yield.

diagnosis: Off-by-one: `balance < amount` lets a user drain their account all the way to `$0` instead of keeping `$1`.
Should be `balance <= amount` so two $80 taps on a $100 wallet fail on the second check.
Returning `{ ok: false }` without `balance` breaks callers expecting a balance field.
Checking `balance < amount` runs before `getBalance` finishes resolving.
fix: Change `balance < amount` to `balance <= amount`.
Include `balance` in the failure object: `return { ok: false, balance };`.
Throw an Error when `balance < amount` instead of returning `{ ok: false }`.
Check `balance - amount < 0` on line 4 instead of `balance < amount`.

diagnosis: Returning `balance - amount` returns the stale local arithmetic instead of reading back the DB row.
Line 6 subtracts `amount` a second time, returning `-$60` after line 5 already deducted `$80`.
`balance - amount` is not rounded to cents, so JS floats return `19.99999999`.
Returning `{ ok: true }` before `setBalance` finishes makes the UI show the old balance.
fix: Return `balance` directly since line 5 already updated it.
Round with `Number((balance - amount).toFixed(2))`.
Re-query `await db.getBalance(userId)` for the return value.
Save `const next = balance - amount` so you don't subtract twice.

diagnosis: Missing `finally` block leaves the DB connection open after throwing on line 2.
Nothing rolls back the balance if the caller disconnects after line 6.
Closing brace ends the `async` function without resolving the outer transaction.
Missing semicolon after `}` causes bundling errors in Node.
fix: Add a `finally { await db.close(); }` block before the closing brace.
Add `return { ok: false };` as a fallback before `}`.
Wrap the whole body in `try { ... } catch { return { ok: false }; }`.
Export `withdraw` with `module.exports = withdraw;`.
